extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / educated early-18th-century coffee-house public (gentlemen, wits, lawyers, officers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars relevant to composing short, satirical/observational periodical essays (Spectator-style): social commentary, literary criticism, and topical news delivered for a coffee‑house audience. Emphasis on manners, moralizing remarks, and witty exempla.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority given in proportion to men's advancement in wisdom and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "superiority is there given in proportion to men's advancement in wisdom and learning; and that just rule of life is so universally received among those happy people, that you shall see an earl walk bareheaded to the son of the meanest artificer, in respect to seven years more worth and knowledge than the nobleman is possessed of."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an evaluative social standard: rank and honour should follow learning and wisdom rather than fortune. The passage models a criterion for praise/admiration in social description — value intellectual merit and portray institutions (here Oxford) as rewarding understanding over wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use learned/astronomical authority to justify institutional dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that the University's almanack (Oxonian computation) is correct because of learned observation: "the cold has been so severe this last winter ... that it retarded the earth in moving round ... full seven days and two seconds" and even that a comet "gave [the earth] a shog" — therefore the term should commence per Oxford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify a procedural/legal position (term commencement) and to satirize disputes about calendrical authority. Shows a criterion for establishing institutional timing: appeal to learned/scientific authority (and its social consequences — forfeited recognisances, nonsuited actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in duels: equality of arms and oversight by seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your men of nice honour ... used seconds, who were to see that all was upon the square, and make a faithful report of the whole combat"; "the swords of those days being pretty long ... the principals put on their pumps, and stripped to their shirts, to show they had nothing but what men of honour carry about them"; "the weapons were always equal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A multipart standard for honourable single combat: ensure equal weapons, visible absence of concealed advantages (stripping to shirts), and use of seconds to witness and report. Presented both descriptively and as a normative ideal governing acceptable conduct in duels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pistols or alternative methods when physical advantages exist
rubrics_metrics.description: "Then, sir, they fought with pistols." (in answer to an active, adroit, strong man insulting an awkward or feeble swordsman). Also debate about cloak-with-pistols as a scruple for men of 'nice honour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inequality of skill/strength makes swords unfair, switching to pistols or other prescribed measures is presented as the means to equalize chances — a practical standard for preserving the appearance of fairness in duel customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of yielding: first disarmed/killed yields (concession of victory)
rubrics_metrics.description: "it was a law among the combatants, that the party which happened to have the first man disarmed or killed, should yield as vanquished;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit procedural criterion for adjudicating the outcome of a combat: the first to be disarmed or killed constitutes the vanquished side. Used to explain how fashions in combat affected incentives and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private conscience condemns trickery as murder despite public forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am of opinion, that one can get no honour in killing a man ... when they have a trick to make the game secure, though they seem to play upon the square." "In truth ... I think such a fact must be murder in a man's own private conscience, whatever it may appear to the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral standard distinguishing legal/formal compliance from true honour: even if a duel follows outward rules, use of tricks to secure victory violates honour and is morally akin to murder. This is an evaluative principle the essay uses to judge practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between fool and madman (criterion for legal/psychological capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mr. Locke has somewhere made a distinction between a madman and a fool: a fool is he that from right principles makes a wrong conclusion; but a madman is one who draws a just inference from false principles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual distinction is presented as a criterion relevant to legal treatment and guardianship (fools in care of the Crown, lunatics in Chancery). It provides a mental-capacity standard used to discuss who should be under what custodial regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of true 'love' as protective, selfless care
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is that sort of passion which truly deserves the name of 'love,' and has something more generous than friendship itself; for it has a constant care of the object beloved, abstracted from its own interests in the possession of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normative definition used to evaluate literary portrayals of passion: love should be represented as guardian/protective concern for the beloved's safety rather than mere possession or self-interested desire. The essay cites Suckling and Milton as exemplars of this portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of tenderness: protective contemplation rather than sensual appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: Example from Suckling: lover steals into his mistress's chamber, contemplates her safety (sleep as image of death) rather than yielding to passion; Milton's "Adam with looks of cordial love / Hung over her enamoured."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for literary depiction of tenderness and love: emphasize contemplative, protective gestures and reverent imagery. These are held up as models for what 'love' writing should aim to convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and invention in battle/military reports enliven narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: "Much might be said for the improvement of this system; which, for its style and invention, may instruct generals and their historians, both in fighting a battle, and describing it when it is over. These elegant expressions, 'Ditto,' 'And so,' 'But soon,' ... do certainly give great life and spirit to the relation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit (partly ironic) praise of lively, repetitive connective phrasing as a means to give 'life and spirit' to a battle account. The passage functions as guidance for composing vivid procedural or event narratives — favour energetic, dynamic phrasing to animate a report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion governs modes of behaviour and affects reputational evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am of opinion, Mr. Sage, that fashion governs a very pretty fellow; nature, or common sense, your ordinary persons, and sometimes men of fine parts." Also discussion of how fashions changed duel practices and what was considered honourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociocultural criterion: when evaluating conduct or character, account for the influence of fashion — what is praised, censured, or considered 'in mode' often reflects changing fashions rather than fixed moral standards. Useful for social commentary in periodical writing.
